title: Guidelines for Seizure Prophylaxis in Patients with Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Statement for Healthcare Professionals from the Neurocritical Care Society

recommendations.section: PICO 1: Antiseizure medication vs. no antiseizure medication in aneurysmal SAH - Recommendation
recommendations.classNote: Either option (no preference for or against)
recommendations.text: Given the uncertainty in benefits and harms, we suggest that prophylactic ASM be used or withheld in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence).

In clinical practice, ASM prophylaxis may be considered for patients at high risk of early seizures, including those with high-grade SAH, anterior circulation aneurysms, intraparenchymal hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus requiring cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) diversion, or those undergoing aneurysm clipping. EEG findings may also guide prophylaxis decisions.

recommendations.classNote: Either option (no preference between agents) — For
recommendations.text: We suggest either prophylactic levetiracetam or phenytoin/fosphenytoin in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence).

Despite limited comparative evidence, levetiracetam is generally preferred due to its favorable safety profile and fewer drug interactions. The observed differences in early seizure prevention could be attributable to appropriate dosing of ASM. Thus, higher dosing may be considered in patients with augmented renal clearance.

recommendations.section: PICO 3: Long (> 3 days) vs. short (<= 3 days) duration of prophylaxis - Recommendation
recommendations.classNote: Either option (individualize; no preference for short or long)
recommendations.text: Regarding the duration of antiseizure medications, because of the uncertainty of benefits and harm, we suggest that the decision to use either short- or long-term therapy with ASM as prophylaxis in adult patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage be individualized to each patient (conditional recommendation, moderate quality of evidence).

A short course (<= 3 days) is generally favored unless EEG or clinical features suggest ongoing seizure risk or high-risk EEG findings. Prophylactic ASM should not be continued beyond 3 days in patients without seizure.

With the current data, many practitioners may use short-term (e.g., until aneurysm is secured, or for up to 3 days) ASM prophylaxis particularly in patients with high risk of early seizures, including those with higher-grade SAH, anterior circulation aneurysms, concomitant intraparenchymal clot, hydrocephalus requiring CSF diversion, or those undergoing clipping versus coiling.

An additional consideration is the use of continuous EEG monitoring, when available, to guide ASM prophylaxis. Practitioners may consider ASM prophylaxis if EEG demonstrates high risk patterns, which may include rhythmic and periodic patterns (excluding generalized rhythmic delta) at > 2 Hz, sporadic epileptiform discharges, lateralized periodic discharges, or lateralized rhythmic delta activity; superimposed plus features as defined by the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society; and brief ictal rhythmic discharges.

If electing to use ASM prophylaxis, practitioners prefer levetiracetam due to better safety profile and tolerability and fewer drug-drug interactions; phenytoin/fosphenytoin induces CYP3A4 and may cause subtherapeutic nimodipine levels. Levetiracetam is generally dosed initially at 500 mg two times a day, although higher maintenance doses of 750-1000 mg two times a day may be considered, particularly in light of the potential for augmented renal clearance commonly observed in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage patients.

If prophylactic ASM is used, we consider using a short course. Thereafter, ASM prophylaxis may be continued using EEG monitoring for guidance. High-risk features on EEG (e.g., high 2HELPS2B score) may be used to guide ASM prophylaxis for a longer duration. We do not favor using ASM prophylaxis beyond 3 days in patients with SAH who do not have clinical or electrographic seizures or high-risk EEG findings.

For patients with confirmed clinical or electrographic seizures, we consider continuing ASM treatment at hospital discharge, with close-interval follow-up within 3 months to guide further ASM management.
